finding: Round 5 keyed `TP_ROUND_DIR` to the cycle (`.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND`) while leaving `seq` and the run totals run-scoped (§3.5: "totals therefore restart at zero on a new run"). A second run over an interrupted round therefore restarts `seq` at the same numbers inside a directory that already holds the first run's files: a re-run role writes `$TP_ROUND_DIR/$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` over — or beside — the dead run's file for that same role. This breaks §3.1's own guarantee that a fresh `seq` "reuses no artifact path", breaks §6.3's "which holds exactly their own round's files", and lets the record unit merge the same role twice under two seqs (double-counting the round that §8a's clustered-count work exists to keep honest). §3.1's retry cleanup only removes the failed attempt's files within the live run, so it cannot cover this.
suggestion: Either make the seq allocator round-scoped and durable (derive the next seq from the highest seq already present in `$TP_ROUND_DIR`), or make a run's first action for a round reconcile that directory: keep at most one file per role id and delete the rest. State the chosen rule in §3.1 and add a test alongside 36 for a role re-run after a driver death.

finding: The two definitions of an `audit-fix` unit's id still disagree in the current text: §3.1 says "the finding index for `audit-fix`", while §3.3's closing paragraph says "`audit-fix`'s `id` is the finding's `(role, item_id)` from the round's merged results". A round's merged results are deduped and re-sorted, so a positional index and a (role,item_id) key are not interchangeable — an index also breaks the §4.2 rule that a success clears `last_failure` only when `(unit_kind, unit_id)` matches, because indices shift between rounds. An implementer cannot pick one without inventing the contract.
suggestion: Delete the "finding index" wording from §3.1 and make it point at §3.3's `(role, item_id)` definition (or the reverse), so exactly one sentence in the spec defines the id.

finding: §3.1 defines an `audit-fix` unit's id as "the finding index", while §3.3 (also modified this round) defines it as "the finding's `(role, item_id)` from the round's merged results". Both sections were rewritten in round 5 and now give two incompatible identities for the same key — the key that `(kind, id)` uniqueness, `last_failure` clearing (§4.2) and the per-unit artifact names all depend on. A positional index is also not stable across a re-merge, so the two definitions are not merely worded differently.
suggestion: Delete "the finding index for `audit-fix`" from §3.1's list and point at §3.3's `(role, item_id)` definition (or state it inline in the same form), so exactly one section defines the id.

finding: §3.1 pins a precise child-environment contract — eight variables (TP_RUN_ID, TP_UNIT_ID, TP_UNIT_KIND, TP_UNIT_SEQ, TP_ROUND, TP_RUN_DIR, TP_ROUND_DIR, TP_FILE), TP_RUN_ID being a ULID, TP_RUN_DIR being an absolute path, TP_ROUND_DIR being .tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND, and children spawned in the repository root — and §10 contains no test for any of it. Test 20 asserts only that runner.env cannot override TP_UNATTENDED, yet §3.1 says the other eight are 'applied on the same terms', so the override protection for them is also unasserted. This is the mechanism the whole design rests on (a unit addresses its artifacts without prose), and every part of it is directly observable through the TP_RUNNER fake.
suggestion: Add a §10.1 test: the fake runner dumps its environment and cwd; assert all eight variables are present with the documented values (TP_RUN_ID matches the ULID charset/length, TP_RUN_DIR absolute and equal to .tp/runs/$TP_RUN_ID, TP_ROUND_DIR equal to .tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND, TP_FILE the resolved task file, cwd the repo root), and that a runner.env entry for each of the eight is overridden by the driver.

finding: The driver must set `TP_ROUND` and derive `TP_ROUND_DIR` = `.tp/rounds/<base>/<phase>-r$TP_ROUND` for every child (§3.1), but `next_units` entries carry only `{kind, id, brief_command}` and §4.1 never says the round number or the phase is available on the oracle payload for the unit about to run. For `review-role`/`audit-role` units the id is the role id, so the round is not recoverable from the entry; for record units the id is a round number, but the spec does not say whether that is the round being recorded or the next one. An implementer has to guess whether to read `phase`/round off some other `tp resume` field, or to compute "current round + 1" itself — and getting it wrong points every role file at the wrong directory.
suggestion: Either add `round` (and `phase`) to each `next_units` entry, or state explicitly which existing `tp resume --json` fields the driver reads for the round and phase, and define the round semantics for a role unit (the round it is producing) versus a record unit.

finding: §4.1 defines the driver's only machine surface — `next_units` as an ordered array of {kind, id, brief_command}, the invariant that a non-concurrent kind is never returned alongside another unit, and next_action.command/brief_command/payload rendering next_units[0] — and §10 has no test for the shape, the ordering, the never-alongside invariant, or the next_action mirroring. Test 2 asserts only that the loop reaches `converged`; test 7 asserts only that an empty array yields no-units. §10.6 mentions the field exists but assertion-moving is not coverage. Equally, §4.1's two distinct empty cases (blocked phase, phase awaiting an operator decision) and the claim that next_action.summary names what the phase is waiting for are untested.
suggestion: Add §10.1/§10.2 tests: (a) for each phase, `tp resume --json` returns next_units entries carrying exactly {kind,id,brief_command} in the documented order; (b) when the head unit's kind is non-concurrent the array has length 1; (c) next_action.command/brief_command/payload equal the rendering of next_units[0]; (d) a blocked phase and an operator-decision phase each yield [] plus a summary naming the wait, and both stop the run with no-units.

finding: §5.1 guarantees "no unattended unit reaches those decisions through a supported route", and names only two hatches it cannot cover (stripping TP_UNATTENDED, editing config through a shell). But §7 states the resolution precedence as CLI > env > task override > project config > built-in, so the env layer is a first-class, supported route to raise review_max_rounds / audit_max_rounds / run_max_*: a unit can prefix any tp invocation with the env override and never touch a file or `tp set --workflow`. §6.2's write denial covers .tp/config.json, .tp/local.json and *.tasks.json but has nothing to say about environment.
suggestion: Extend §5.1 to the env layer explicitly: under TP_UNATTENDED, an env-supplied value for a fenced field that exceeds the value resolved without it is refused (exit 2) on the same terms as `tp set --workflow`, and add a test alongside test 19. Otherwise the guarantee sentence must be narrowed to "through the CLI or a supported file write".

finding: §6.2 states the Stop hook 'must consult `stop_hook_active` and block at most once per unit', and calls a hook that always blocks 'the loop this whole version exists to make terminating'. Test 26 asserts only the two first-invocation outcomes (does not block with an escalation record, does block with neither the durable write nor a record); nothing asserts the once-only property. The termination guarantee of the whole design is therefore the one hook behaviour with no pass/fail test.
suggestion: Add to §10.4: invoke the Stop hook twice for the same unit with the durable write still absent and stop_hook_active true on the second call; assert the first blocks with the reason and the second permits stop. Also assert the block reason names the missing durable write for that kind.

finding: §8a's arity item justifies moving arity violations to exit 2 so "a driver can separate a mistyped invocation from a failed one without reading the message", but this same spec overloads exit 2 with two non-usage meanings: §5.1 makes every refused user-only decision exit 2, and §5.2 makes a normal, expected escalation exit 2 ("The record, not the exit code, is the signal"). After this release a driver seeing exit 2 cannot tell a typo from a refusal from a planned escalation by exit code alone, so the stated benefit of the arity change does not hold within the spec that asks for it.
suggestion: Either state explicitly that exit 2 is disambiguated by artifact presence (escalation record) and hint payload, and drop the claim that exit 2 alone separates a mistyped invocation from a failure, or give escalation its own exit code distinct from the usage code and keep exit 2 for genuine usage errors.

finding: Test 5 — 'Role units run concurrently and every other kind does not overlap them' — names no deterministic observable. One engineer asserts wall-clock overlap of child start/end timestamps (inherently racy: on a loaded machine two genuinely concurrent children can serialize), another asserts that all children were spawned before any was waited on, a third asserts only that the run state holds N rows for one iteration. Concurrency is the claim most likely to yield a flaky or vacuous test, and §3.3 supplies no observable the fake runner is required to emit.
suggestion: Pin the mechanism: require the fake runner to write a start marker, wait for a barrier file, and write an end marker, so the test asserts a deterministic interleaving (all N starts precede any end for role units; for every other kind the previous unit's end precedes the next unit's start). State this in §10.1 test 1's description of the seam.

finding: Tests 35 and 6 both require a `crashed` run — run_state `crashed` is defined as 'stop_reason unset and .tp/locks/run-<base>.lock not held' — but nothing in the spec says how a test produces that state deterministically. If the driver runs in-process in tests, the lock is released on process exit and stop_reason writing cannot be skipped without a seam; if it must be a killed out-of-process driver, the spec never says the driver is spawnable that way, and SIGKILL-vs-flock-release behaviour differs by platform. Test 6's 'A crashed driver loses nothing' compounds this with a non-assertable predicate ('loses nothing').
suggestion: Name the seam that produces a crash for tests (e.g. an out-of-process driver binary the test SIGKILLs, or a documented fault-injection env var that aborts before the stop write), and restate test 6 as concrete assertions: the round directory retains the collected role files, the wip task is unchanged, and the second run's first unit equals the interrupted unit's (kind, id).

finding: §10.6 says "The `.tp/.gitignore` fixture gains three entries", but test 15 (§10.2) asserts four newly ignored paths: `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/` and `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`. Three of these are introduced by §3.5 and one by §4.2; nothing in the spec says any two share a single pattern. The invalidated-tests section and the test it describes disagree on how many entries the shipped fixture gains.
suggestion: State the exact gitignore entries once (in §3.5 or §4.2) and have §10.6 cite that list rather than a count, or correct "three" to the number of patterns actually added and name them.

finding: §10.6 says "The `.tp/.gitignore` fixture gains three entries", while test 15 asserts four distinct paths are ignored: `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/` and `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json`. Two of those are per-task-file names, so the implementer must also invent the glob form (`run-*.json`, `last_failure-*.json`) — the spec gives the instance names, never the patterns to write.
suggestion: State the literal lines the shipped `.tp/.gitignore` gains (e.g. `run-*.json`, `last_failure-*.json`, `runs/`, `rounds/`) and make §10.6's count match.

finding: §10.6 still says "The `.tp/.gitignore` fixture gains three entries", but test 15 (§10.2) now lists four paths — `.tp/run-<base>.json`, `.tp/runs/`, `.tp/rounds/` and `.tp/last_failure-<base>.json` — and the shipped `.tp/.gitignore` currently holds only `local.json` and `locks/`, so none of the four is already covered. The per-base naming and `.tp/rounds/` both arrived in round 5; the count was not updated with them. A fixture assertion written to the stale number will disagree with the test-15 list.
suggestion: Change "three entries" to four, or drop the count and let test 15's list be the single statement of what the fixture gains.

finding: §3.1 still says a unit's id is "the finding index for `audit-fix`", while §3.3 now says "`audit-fix`'s `id` is the finding's `(role, item_id)` from the round's merged results". These are different identifiers, and §3.1 is the section that makes `(kind, id)` the key `last_failure` clears on (§4.2) — so a positional index there means a fix retry after a re-merge clears the wrong unit's failure. The earlier round's correction landed only in §3.3.
suggestion: Replace "the finding index" in §3.1 with "the finding's `(role, item_id)`", so the id definition reads identically in §3.1, §3.3 and §4.2.

finding: Three required reports name no stream, format or field, so no two engineers write the same assertion: §3.2.2 'reported once at run start, not silently' and 'the run-start report names which kinds are unmetered'; §5.2 'when an iteration produces several, the driver reports the lowest `seq`'; §5.2 'Its exit code is reported and changes nothing' for notify_cmd. Each is a normative observable with no defined channel (stdout? stderr? a run-state field? `--status` output?), and none appears in §3.5's enumeration of what `tp run --status` prints or in the run-state schema.
suggestion: For each, name the channel and the exact carrier: e.g. 'the driver writes one stderr line at run start listing unmetered kinds', 'the escalation stop reports the lowest-seq record path in `tp run --status` as `escalation_path`', 'notify_cmd's exit code is reported as `notify_exit_code` in the run state'. Then add tests asserting those carriers.

finding: §3.2.2 defines spend reading for two cases — a runner that declares a `spend_key` and one that does not — but not the failure case an implementer will hit first: the runner declares a key and the final log line is absent (child killed before writing), is not JSON, or does not hold that dot path. The spec gives no exit code, no hint, and no rule for whether the unit's `spend_usd` becomes null, whether the run continues, and whether a repeated read failure is reported once or per unit. `--status` promises "spend against each cap", which a silent null quietly falsifies.
suggestion: Add one sentence: an unreadable or missing spend key records `spend_usd: null` for that unit, does not fail the unit or the run, and is reported once per run in the same run-start notice that names unmetered kinds.

finding: §3.2/§3.2.1 make four testable claims with no test in §10.2: (1) `runner` takes three shapes — built-in name, object, per-kind map — and a map missing `default` is a usage error (no exit code is even asserted anywhere); (2) the `claude` template's args are an exact literal list; (3) the --max-budget-usd flag pair is appended only when run_max_unit_budget_usd is non-zero and omitted entirely at 0, while a positional template still receives a literal 0; (4) every child is spawned with stdin closed — the §2 lesson row 'backgrounded runs hang on stdin'. Test 10 covers placeholder resolution only.
suggestion: Add §10.2 tests: per-kind map routes audit units to a different cmd while `default` covers the rest and a map without `default` exits 2; the built-in `claude` and `opencode` templates produce their documented argv, with the budget flag present at a non-zero value, absent at 0, and a positional {max_budget_usd} receiving `0`; and a child whose runner reads stdin sees EOF immediately.

finding: Converting every durable-write predicate to an absolute state (round 5) makes two of them satisfiable before the unit runs, so the Stop hook (§6.2) and the driver's success test both pass a unit that did nothing. `decompose`'s "The task file holds at least one task" is already true on any retry after a partially-completed import, so a decompose unit that imports nothing is recorded as success and the run proceeds on an incomplete task set; `review-resolve`'s "Every finding in the round's file carries a disposition" is already true if the round was fully disposed before the unit started. The delta-free property is worth keeping, but the spec asserts these predicates are sufficient (§3.3, test 18) and does not say what stops a no-op unit passing.
suggestion: Keep the predicates absolute but tighten the two that can pre-hold: for `decompose` require the task file to satisfy `tp validate` coverage for the spec (a state), and for `review-resolve` require the round's recorded round file to be marked resolved. Alternatively state explicitly that the oracle never emits these units when their predicate already holds, and test that.

finding: `audit-fix`'s id is a tuple `(role, item_id)`, but every consumer of an id is a flat string: `TP_UNIT_ID` in the child environment (§3.1), the `{unit_id}` placeholder (§3.2.1), the `id` field of a run-state unit row (§3.5), `last_failure.unit_id` (§4.2), and — for role units — the artifact filename `$TP_UNIT_SEQ-$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson` (§6.3). The spec never states how the tuple is rendered as a string, nor what happens when a role id or item_id contains a path separator or whitespace.
suggestion: State the encoding once (e.g. `<role>/<item_id>`, or `<role>:<item_id>` with a named sanitization for path-unsafe characters) and say that ids are sanitized before they reach a filename or an argv template.

finding: §3.3 defines `audit-fix`'s id as the finding's tuple `(role, item_id)`, but the id is consumed as a string in three places with no stated encoding: the log path `$TP_RUN_DIR/<seq>-<kind>-<id>.jsonl` (§3.5), the run-state `id` field (§3.5 schema), and the `{unit_id}` placeholder (§3.2.1). No separator, ordering or escaping is specified, and neither role ids nor item_ids are constrained to path-safe characters, so a role id containing `/` or a space yields a different filename in two implementations — or an escape from TP_RUN_DIR. §3.1's list of ids ('the finding index for audit-fix') and §3.3's tuple also give two different strings for the same unit.
suggestion: Pin one serialization for `audit-fix`'s id (e.g. `<role>:<item_id>`), state the sanitization applied when it becomes a path component, and make §3.1's id list use the same wording as §3.3. Add a test with a role id and item_id containing a path separator and a space asserting the log path stays inside TP_RUN_DIR.

finding: Round 5 moved `converged` to the front of the stop_reason precedence, so a checkpoint that satisfies both `converged` and `escalation` records `converged` and exits 0. That contradicts §5.2, which states a unit that wrote an escalation record "stops the run with `stop_reason: escalation`" and which fires `notify_cmd` only "on every non-converged stop" — the escalation record is then left on disk, un-notified and un-reported, while the run exits successfully. §5.1's whole premise is that a user-only decision must never be resolved by the run itself.
suggestion: Either rank `escalation` above `converged`, or state explicitly in §3.4 that a converged stop still reports every escalation record written in the final iteration and still invokes `notify_cmd`, and reconcile §5.2's wording with it.

finding: `interrupted` is the only stop_reason row with no test. Test 3 covers 'each cap produces its own stop_reason' and interruption is not a cap, so §3.4's three interruption guarantees are unasserted: SIGINT and SIGTERM behave identically, in-flight children run to completion, no new unit is spawned, and the run state is written before the driver exits. The same paragraph's 'caps are evaluated between iterations only, so a run overshoots by at most one iteration; the driver kills nothing' is likewise untested.
suggestion: Add to §10.1: with a fake runner that sleeps, send SIGINT (and a second case, SIGTERM) mid-iteration; assert the in-flight child's row is completed with a real exit_code, no further child is spawned, stop_reason is `interrupted`, and the run state file exists after the driver exits. Add a cap-overshoot test asserting the wall-clock cap trips only between iterations and the running child is not killed.

finding: `tp run --dry-run` "prints the units the driver would execute next and exits without spawning anything" — which is exactly `tp resume --json`'s `next_units`, the array §4.1 makes the driver's only parsed input and §3.1 step 3 consumes verbatim. As specified the flag adds a command surface, an output contract and a test (13) that reproduce an existing one, and it does not promise the one thing a dry run could add that `tp resume` cannot: the resolved runner `cmd`/argv per unit and the resolved cap values.
suggestion: Either drop `--dry-run` and document `tp resume --json` as the preview, or specify that it prints the resolved spawn plan (runner cmd, expanded args with placeholders filled, resolved `run_max_*` values) — which earns the flag because that resolution exists nowhere else — and update test 13 to assert the resolved argv rather than the unit list.

finding: §3.5 says both run-state writes are atomic (temp + rename) 'because concurrent siblings write rows in the same iteration', and that accrued totals restart at zero on a new run. Test 12 covers only the single-unit row lifecycle (null exit_code before, updated after), so neither the concurrent-sibling case nor the totals reset has a test. The concurrency claim is the one place where a lost update is plausible, and it is precisely the case test 12 does not exercise.
suggestion: Add to §10.2: run an iteration with N concurrent role units and assert the final run state holds exactly N rows, each with its own seq/exit_code and none lost or duplicated; and assert a second `tp run` over the same cycle starts totals.units/wall_clock_seconds/spend_usd at zero rather than accumulating the previous run's.

finding: §4.1 says `next_units` is `[]` in two distinct non-releasable cases — a blocked phase and a phase awaiting an operator decision — that both stop the run with `no-units`, and relies on `next_action.summary` to name what the phase is waiting for. But §3.5's `--status` payload enumerates phase, units done, spend against each cap, the last unit's exit code and log path, `stop_reason`, `run_state`, and the audit divergence signals — it never carries `next_action.summary`. The operator of an unattended run therefore sees `no-units` with no way to tell "nothing is runnable" from "your decision is required", which is the same operator-facing gap §1 promises to close for the audit phase.
suggestion: Add `next_action.summary` (or an equivalent `stop_detail`) to the `--status` payload and to `notify_cmd`'s environment on a `no-units` stop, and extend test 14 to assert the two `no-units` causes are distinguishable.

finding: `tp resume --json` now carries the first pending unit twice: `next_units[0]` is the machine surface and `next_action`'s `command`, `brief_command` and `payload` are explicitly a rendering of that same entry. The two have disjoint audiences — the driver parses only `next_units`, the human reads only `next_action` — so no single invocation needs both, and the spec sets no `--compact` rule for either. Every `tp resume` in the loop (step 1 of §3.1, plus the SessionStart hook's `tp resume --compact`) pays for the duplicate.
suggestion: State which of the two `--compact` strips — the natural choice is `next_action`'s rendered fields, since §6.2 bounds the hook payload by compact output and the human summary is the one already covered by `next_action.summary`. Add the assertion to §10.2 test 14 or a new §10.5 item.

finding: §4.2 gives last_failure two write triggers — 'when a unit exits non-zero, or closes with a failed quality gate' — and states that summary is tp-authored (the failing command, and the gate's own output when a gate failed) and that a second failure overwrites the file. Test 23 covers only the non-zero-exit trigger plus surfacing/survival/clearing. The failed-gate trigger, the summary's authorship/content, and the overwrite rule have no test, and the gate trigger is the one that produces a zero-exit failure the exit-code path would miss.
suggestion: Add to §10.3: a unit that closes with a failing quality gate writes last_failure with the gate's own output in `summary` and no child prose; a second, different failure overwrites the single object rather than appending; and assert the object's field set {unit_kind, unit_id, phase, exit_code, summary, at}.

finding: §4.2 has two different writers for one single-object file with no ordering rule: the driver writes it "when a unit exits non-zero", while the gate case ("or closes with a failed quality gate") can only be authored inside the child, since only the child has the gate's output. A gate failure normally also makes the unit exit non-zero, so the driver's later write overwrites the child's — and the driver cannot reconstruct the promised summary ("the gate's own output when a gate failed"). §3.5 explicitly requires atomic writes for run state because concurrent siblings write it; §4.2 says nothing about concurrent failing role units racing on the same path.
suggestion: Name one writer (the driver) and make the gate output reach it through a file the child already writes, or state that a child-authored last_failure is not overwritten by the driver's exit-code record for the same (unit_kind, unit_id). Either way, require the same temp+rename atomicity §3.5 requires, since concurrent role units can fail in one iteration.

finding: Round 5 fenced `tp set --workflow run_max_*=` "above the resolved value", with the rationale that "lowering a budget cannot manufacture convergence". The glob now covers `run_max_budget_usd`, whose 0 is the disabled sentinel (§7, §3.4). Under the rule as written, an unattended unit that sets `run_max_budget_usd=0` is *lowering* the value and is accepted — which removes the budget cap entirely — while setting it from 0 to a real number is "above the resolved value" and is refused, even though it tightens the run. The same inversion applies to `run_max_unit_budget_usd` (0 = flag omitted).
suggestion: Compare against the effective cap rather than the raw number: treat 0 as +infinity for the budget fields, so 0 -> N is accepted and N -> 0 is refused. Say so in §5.1 and cover it in test 19.

finding: The fourth fence row is a glob — "`tp set --workflow run_max_*=` above the resolved value" — but the justifying prose names only `run_max_units` and `run_max_wall_clock_seconds`. It is undecidable from the text whether the fence also covers `run_max_budget_usd`, `run_max_unit_budget_usd` and `run_max_unit_retries`, and it says nothing about the two §7 fields that would let a unit escape the fence by other means: `runner` (which decides what binary every subsequent child is) and `notify_cmd` (an arbitrary command tp execs). §10.3 test 19 tests "the four user-only operations" without pinning the field set either, so the test cannot settle it.
suggestion: Replace the glob with the explicit fenced list, and state the rule for `runner`/`notify_cmd` under `TP_UNATTENDED` (either fenced outright, or explicitly out of scope with a sentence saying why).

finding: §5.1 pins the activation predicate with three boundaries — 'active when the variable is present, non-empty and not `0`' — but test 19 exercises only `TP_UNATTENDED=1` and the variable's absence. Every discriminating value is untested: empty string (inactive), `0` (inactive), `2`/`false`/`no` (active by the stated rule, which is counter-intuitive and the most likely place two implementations diverge). A behavioural test that passes with either an is-set check or a truthy-parse check verifies nothing about the rule.
suggestion: Extend test 19 into a table over TP_UNATTENDED values {unset, "", "0", "1", "2", "false"} asserting active/inactive per §5.1's rule for at least one fenced operation.

finding: §5.1 fences four user-only decisions, the fourth being `tp set --workflow run_max_*=` above the resolved value. §5.2's `decision` enum is `skip-gate`, `raise-review-cap`, `raise-audit-cap`, `import-force` or `other` — it has a named value for three of the four fences and none for the run caps, so the one decision this version introduces is the one that can only be escalated as `other`. Since §5.2 says an escalation is the supported route out of a refusal, the enum and the fence table should be the same four items.
suggestion: Add `raise-run-cap` to the §5.2 enum (keeping `other` for everything else), and state that each §5.1 refusal hint names the matching `--decision` value so the refused unit knows which escalation to write.

finding: §5.2 says `decision` is one of `skip-gate`, `raise-review-cap`, `raise-audit-cap`, `import-force` or `other`, but never states what happens when a unit passes a value outside that set — rejected as a usage error, accepted verbatim, or coerced to `other`. Test 22 does not cover it. The consequence is not cosmetic: if an out-of-enum value is accepted, the record still stops the run with `escalation` and the unit is not counted as a failed attempt, so the enumeration is decorative; if rejected, the unit becomes an ordinary failure. Two engineers write opposite tests.
suggestion: State the behaviour explicitly ('a `--decision` outside the set is a usage error, exit 2, and writes no record') and add it to test 22 alongside an assertion that no escalation record is left behind in that case.

finding: The plugin "preflights: if `tp` is absent from `PATH` or older than `0.35.0`, it fails with the install command rather than degrading quietly", but §6.2's hook table declares only three events (`SessionStart`, `PreToolUse`, `Stop`) and none of them is the preflight. The spec does not say where the check runs, what "fails" means to a Claude Code session (blocking output, non-zero exit, injected context), how `tp --version` output is parsed, or how the comparison against `plugin.json`'s version is done for a prerelease or dev-build version string.
suggestion: Attach the preflight to a named event (most naturally the `SessionStart` hook, before the `tp resume --compact` payload), state its failure mode in the hook's own terms, and pin the version comparison rule (semver compare against `plugin.json.version`, unparseable output treated as too old).

finding: The Stop hook must decide, inside a 10-second timeout (§6.4) and without reading run state, whether the current unit's durable write exists — for all eight kinds. Two of the eight predicates are trivially checkable (`$TP_ROUND_DIR/...ndjson` exists), but the rest are not addressable from the environment the hook has: "a review/audit round file for `$TP_ROUND` exists" names no path under `.tp-review/`, "every finding in the round's file carries a disposition" and "that finding's row is recorded resolved" name no field, and "the task's `status` is `done`" requires resolving and parsing `$TP_FILE`. The spec offers no tp command that answers "is this unit's durable write present?", so the hook has to reimplement and re-derive eight predicates in shell — the exact duplication §3.3 says it wants to avoid by having the hook and the driver read "the same condition".
suggestion: Give the predicate one owner: a tp subcommand (e.g. `tp run --check-unit`, reading `TP_UNIT_KIND`/`TP_UNIT_ID`/`TP_ROUND_DIR`/`TP_FILE` and exiting 0/1) that both the driver's success test and the hook invoke; state that the hook's whole logic is that call plus the escalation-file test.

finding: §6.2 says the Stop hook's durable write is "the state that kind names in §3.3's fourth column". §3.3's table columns are Kind | Ends in | Durable write | Concurrency — the durable write is the third column; the fourth is Concurrency. A hook written from the citation reads the wrong column, and the Stop hook is the one component §3.3 explicitly promises reads the same condition as the driver.
suggestion: Change the reference to "§3.3's `Durable write` column" — naming the column rather than its ordinal, so a later column insertion cannot re-break it.

finding: §6.2 says the Stop hook's durable write is "the state that kind names in §3.3's fourth column". §3.3's table columns are Kind | Ends in | Durable write | Concurrency — the durable-write predicate is the **third** column; the fourth is Concurrency. An implementer following the reference literally wires the hook to the wrong column.
suggestion: Change the reference to "§3.3's `Durable write` column" — name the column rather than its position, so a future column insertion cannot re-break it.

finding: §6.4 requires every shipped hook to declare a `timeout` of 10 seconds and to exit non-zero rather than hang, calling it 'the one failure mode in this design that the driver cannot observe from outside' — and §10.4 has no test for it. §6.1's preflight is in the same position: 'if tp is absent from PATH or older than 0.35.0, it fails with the install command', with the minimum being plugin.json's own version compared against `tp --version`, is untested and the comparison semantics are unpinned (how a prerelease or a dev-build version string compares).
suggestion: Add to §10.4: assert each hook entry in the shipped hook config declares timeout 10; assert a hook whose helper cannot complete exits non-zero. Add a preflight test over a fake `tp` on PATH at an older version, an absent `tp`, and an equal version, and state the comparison rule (semver, prerelease treated as lower).

finding: Test 16 says 'Each §7 field takes its documented default, accepts both range endpoints, and rejects one step outside each', but two of the seven fields have no endpoints: `runner`'s Range column reads 'Built-in name or object' and `notify_cmd`'s reads 'Any command string'. 'One step outside' is undefined for both, so the test is not writable as stated. The same test also omits the env layer from the precedence chain it checks (it asserts CLI > task override > project config only) and never exercises §7's stated exception that TP_RUNNER outranks every layer including CLI. Separately, §7's last sentence — 'Under --compact, stop_reason and the cap totals survive; per-unit rows and log paths are stripped' — names no command (presumably `tp run --status --compact`) and has no test at all.
suggestion: Split test 16: numeric fields get default + both endpoints + one step outside each; `runner` gets a valid-name / valid-object / invalid-shape triple; `notify_cmd` gets set/unset. Add the env layer to the precedence assertion and a case where TP_RUNNER beats an explicit CLI flag. Name the command carrying --compact in §7 and add a test asserting the surviving and stripped keys.

finding: The `inputs` array is added to every `--merge` payload for both `tp review --merge` and `tp audit --merge`, one entry per input file, on clean rounds as well as broken ones — yet the same paragraph states the decision it exists for is carried by the exit code alone ("an unattended driver reads the exit code alone"). On a healthy 5-role round that is five `{path, parsed, skipped}` objects with `skipped: 0` that no consumer branches on, and §7's `--compact` rule covers only run state, so nothing strips them.
suggestion: Emit `inputs` entries only for files with `skipped > 0` (plus the all-lines-skipped case that drives exit 1), or state explicitly that `inputs` is stripped under `--compact`. Add the compact/omission rule to §8a and an assertion to test 32 that a fully clean merge carries no per-file rows.

finding: The dropped-role rule is stated as 'an input with at least one line, none of which parsed, makes --merge exit 1' while 'a zero-byte file stays the documented way a role reports nothing found and keeps exiting 0'. The boundary between the two is undecidable for the realistic middle cases: a file containing only a newline, or only blank/whitespace lines, has at least one line and zero parsed lines, so by the literal rule it exits 1 — yet it is the same 'role found nothing' intent as a zero-byte file, and a shell redirect commonly produces it. Test 32 tests only the two extremes, so both implementations pass it.
suggestion: Define the counted population explicitly ('blank and whitespace-only lines are ignored; exit 1 requires at least one non-blank line and zero parsed rows') and extend test 32 with a newline-only file and a whitespace-lines-only file asserting exit 0.

finding: `location_clusters` is added to both `tp review --merge` and `--status`, and the same paragraph guarantees it changes nothing the driver acts on: convergence arithmetic, the stored `clean` flag and the `--status --check` exit code are all unchanged. So the defect it was raised for (a driver reading clustered duplicates as rounds remaining) is untouched, and the new bytes feed no decision an agent makes — one entry per multi-role location, which on the measured round-nine data is dozens of `{location, roles[], severities[], count}` objects on every merge and every status call.
suggestion: Either name the decision it feeds and where (operator-facing `--status` only, and omitted when empty), or drop it from the `--merge` payload and keep it in `--status`. Test 28 should assert it is absent when no location has findings from more than one role.

finding: §8a opens "Four measured defects in the signals an unattended driver consumes" and cites four measurement sources (candidates §1, §3, §7, §10), but the section then carries five bolded required behaviours: clustered counts, phase-honest mechanization advice, truncated audits, a dropped role that merges clean, and arity violations as usage errors. §10.5 correspondingly asserts five items (tests 28-32). The count and the citation list are one short of the content, leaving it undecided whether the fifth item is in scope or leftover.
suggestion: Change the opening to "Five measured defects" and add the fifth measurement's source section, or move the item that has no measurement out of §8a into its own subsection so the count, the citations and the bolded list agree.

finding: §8a states arity violations should exit 2 "matching §9's definition of a usage error". §9 is the Non-Goals list and defines nothing about exit codes; the usage-error definition is tp's existing exit-code invariant (0 success, 1 validation, 2 usage, 3 file, 4 state) documented in skills/tp/REFERENCE.md, not in this spec. An implementer following the citation finds no definition to match.
suggestion: Replace "§9's definition of a usage error" with a citation of the existing exit-code contract (REFERENCE.md's exit-code table), or state the code meanings inline in §8a.

finding: Test 12 says "A run.json row exists with null `exit_code` before its child exits", using the pre-namespacing filename; §3.5 now names the file `.tp/run-<base>.json` and test 15 uses that form. A stale unnamespaced name in the test list is the kind of reference that survives into an implementation asserting the wrong path.
suggestion: Rewrite test 12 as "A `.tp/run-<base>.json` row exists with null `exit_code` …".

finding: Of the eight variables every child is spawned with, `TP_RUN_ID` has no named consumer inside a unit and is exactly derivable from one that does: `TP_RUN_DIR` is defined as the absolute path of `.tp/runs/$TP_RUN_ID`, so `basename(TP_RUN_DIR)` is the id. Every artifact path in the spec (escalation record, log path, `$TP_ROUND_DIR`) is expressed against `TP_RUN_DIR` or `TP_ROUND_DIR`, and the only other place `TP_RUN_ID` appears is `notify_cmd`'s environment (§5.2), which the driver sets separately.
suggestion: Drop `TP_RUN_ID` from the child environment and keep it in `notify_cmd`'s, or name the child-side consumer that needs it as a value rather than as a path component. If it stays, say so as a convenience alias so no reader has to look for the missing use.

finding: `spend_key` is specified as a "dot path to the cost field", but every case the spec names is a top-level key: `claude` uses `total_cost_usd`, the `TP_RUNNER` seam uses `total_cost_usd`, and `opencode` declares none. Nothing exercises a nested path — §10.2 test 11 only covers present-vs-absent — so the dot-path grammar is a parser and a class of resolution failures (path missing, resolves to a non-number) bought for a capability no configuration in this release uses.
suggestion: Specify `spend_key` as a plain key name in the final log line and widen it only when a real runner needs nesting; if the dot path stays, add a test with a nested key so the generality is at least paid for by coverage.

finding: Two mechanisms defend the same collision. §3.1 makes cleanup mandatory — "Before retrying, the driver removes the failed attempt's files from the round directory, leaving only successful role files for the merge" — and separately prefixes every role artifact with `$TP_UNIT_SEQ`. With the cleanup in force the prefix buys nothing, but it costs: `TP_UNIT_SEQ` must then be threaded into the child environment (§3.1), the Stop hook's escalation predicate (§6.2), the agent write allowlist (§6.3) and the emitted filename `tp review`/`tp audit` produce under `TP_ROUND_DIR` (§6.3) — four places that must agree on one name.
suggestion: Pick one: keep the seq prefix and drop the pre-retry cleanup requirement (the merge then needs a rule for which attempt wins), or keep the cleanup and name role files `$TP_UNIT_ID.ndjson`, which removes `TP_UNIT_SEQ` from the role path in all four places. Escalation records still need the seq prefix for concurrent siblings, so that use is unaffected.

finding: Round 5 rewrote the retry paragraph to end "`totals.units` and `--status`'s units-done count attempts too, so all three counters read the same number", but the sentence names only two counters; the third (`run_max_units`) lives in the table row above and is never named here. Test 33 names all three, so the prose is the weaker statement of the same rule.
suggestion: Name the third explicitly: "…so `run_max_units`, `totals.units` and `--status`'s units-done all read the same number."

finding: §3.4 says caps are evaluated between iterations only, so "a run can overshoot its wall-clock and budget caps by at most one iteration" — but the same evaluation point lets `run_max_units` overshoot as well: one iteration spawns a whole role fan-out at once (§3.3), and with attempts counted (§3.4, test 33) a run can exceed `run_max_units` by up to the number of active roles minus one. The sentence names only two of the three caps that can be exceeded.
suggestion: Extend the overshoot sentence to all three caps and bound it explicitly ("by at most one iteration's fan-out"), so an operator sizing `run_max_units` knows the effective ceiling.

finding: `tp escalate`'s repeated `--option <text>` flag and the resulting `options[]` array are written into the escalation record and then read by nothing the spec describes: the driver reports the lowest-`seq` record and stops, `notify_cmd` receives only `TP_ESCALATION_PATH`, and §10.3 test 22 asserts the record, the exit code, the sibling isolation and the outside-a-run error but never an option. `evidence` is already free text a human reads, so a second free-text channel on the same object is surface the unit must produce with no decision downstream of it.
suggestion: Either drop `--option`/`options[]` and let `evidence` carry the alternatives, or state what consumes the array (e.g. `tp run --status` rendering the choices to the operator) and assert it in test 22.

finding: §7's `runner` row gives the range as "Built-in name or object", but §3.2 defines three accepted shapes — a built-in template name, a runner object, or a map from unit kind to either with a required `default` key. The per-kind map is the shape §3.2 spends a paragraph justifying, and §7 is the section `tp validate --project` is said to cover "on the same terms as every existing workflow field", so validation written from the table rejects the map.
suggestion: Change the range cell to "Built-in name, runner object, or per-kind map (with `default`)" and state that a map missing `default` is the usage error §3.2 already names.
